senses.definition: The quality of being decent; propriety.

quotes.text: Immodest words admit of no defence, / For want of decency is want of sense.
quotes.reference: 1684, Wentworth Dillon, An Essay on Translated Verse:

quotes.text: Indeed it is for the moſt part in our ſkill in manners, and in the obſervances of time and place, and of decency in general, which is only to be learned in thoſe ſchools to which Horace recommends us, that what is called Taſte by way of diſtinction, conſiſts; and which is in reality no other than a more refined judgment.
quotes.reference: 1757 (date written), [Edmund Burke], “Introduction. On Taste.”, in A Philosophical Enquiry into the Origin of Our Ideas of the Sublime and Beautiful, 2nd edition, London: […] R[obert] and J[ames] Dodsley, […], published 1759, →OCLC, part, page 30:

quotes.text: [To Joseph McCarthy:] Have you no sense of decency, sir? At long last, have you left no sense of decency?
quotes.reference: 1954 June, Joseph N. Welch, Army–McCarthy hearings:

quotes.text: Now, what is interesting about that poem is nothing. But, what is relevant about it is that his muse is his wife, Marcela, who is 42 years younger than him. He is 75, she is 33. And I’ll say this, at least when 70-something American politicians get creepily handsy with 30-something women, they have the decency to do so with their own daughters. Have some class, Brazil! Have some class!
quotes.reference: 2016, Tim Carvell [et al.], “Journalism”, in Last Week Tonight with John Oliver, season 3, episode 20, John Oliver (actor), Warner Bros. Television, via HBO:

senses.definition: That which is proper or becoming.

quotes.text: Those thousand decencies, that daily flow / From all her words and actions.
